title: Coca-Cola vs. PepsiCo
subtitle: The same cola rivalry, fought by two companies that made very different choices about what to own: one mostly sells concentrate to independent bottlers and tends its brands, the other makes, bottles and delivers much of what it sells and takes most of its revenue from foods.
cardSubtitle: Two colas made the same way, very different businesses behind them.

keyHighlights.title: Selling the Syrup
keyHighlights.description: Concentrate operations made up 59% of Coca-Cola's revenue in fiscal 2025.

keyHighlights.title: A Food Company Too
keyHighlights.description: Convenient foods made up 58% of PepsiCo's fiscal 2025 net revenue, beverages 42%.

keyHighlights.title: Revenue Versus Margin
keyHighlights.description: Both filings say finished drinks generally bring more revenue but thinner margins than selling concentrate.

In the can, the two famous colas are made the same basic way, from a flavour concentrate, sweetener and carbonated water.

content.text: The companies behind the cans are not twins at all. One mostly sells the flavour and the name, and leaves the heavy lifting to partners. The other makes, bottles and delivers a large share of what it sells, and takes most of its revenue from chips, cereals and other foods.

content.text: Coca-Cola began in Atlanta in 1886 as a syrup, mixed with carbonated water at a pharmacy soda fountain. In a sense it never stopped being a syrup company. Its annual report describes two lines of business: concentrate operations, selling concentrate and syrup to bottlers, and finished product operations, selling finished drinks.

content.text: Most of its drinks are made and sold by independent bottlers. Under its bottler's agreements, a bottler generally buys concentrate from Coca-Cola or a supplier it authorizes, then adds water and sweetener, packages the drink and sells it in an assigned territory. In fiscal 2025 the five largest accounted for 44% of worldwide volume.

Owning less, on purpose

content.text: Concentrate operations made up 59% of Coca-Cola's revenue of about $47.9 billion in fiscal 2025, and 85% of its unit case volume. Finished drinks were the other 15% of volume but 41% of revenue. The filing states the trade-off plainly: finished drinks generally bring in more revenue for the volume sold, but at lower gross margins.

content.text: So it has repeatedly sold company-owned bottling to independent partners, which it calls refranchising. In 2025 it refranchised bottling in parts of India, and agreed to sell part of its stake in its African bottling business to one of its largest bottlers, keeping 25%.

content.text: Coca-Cola's own history shows how strongly drinkers are attached to the brand. In April 1985 it changed its formula for the first time in 99 years, after taste tests with nearly 200,000 consumers. Following a wave of consumer protest, the original formula came back 79 days later as Coca-Cola classic.

A Europe, Middle East and Africa unit running both foods and company-owned bottlers
Food-only units for Latin America and Asia Pacific

content.text: Where Coca-Cola mostly leaves bottling to partners, PepsiCo does much of it itself. Its North American drinks business runs its own bottling plants, and direct store delivery, run with its bottlers and distributors, carries drinks and foods straight to stores, where its staff or bottlers stock the shelves. In fiscal 2025, company-owned bottlers produced 36% of its revenue.

content.text: The cost shows in the filings. In fiscal 2025 PepsiCo took in roughly twice Coca-Cola's revenue, but it employed about 306,000 people against Coca-Cola's 65,900, more than four times as many.

content.text: Each structure buys something. Running its own bottling and store delivery gives PepsiCo a direct hand in how its drinks and foods are stocked and displayed on store shelves. Selling concentrate gives Coca-Cola a leaner business built on its brands, but leaves it reliant on bottlers that are independent contractors, not its agents.

content.text: Two companies can sell products made the same way and still be very different businesses. The model lives in two lines of the annual report: where the revenue comes from, and who owns the plants and the trucks.

content.text: Some caveats. Coca-Cola's lean figures leave out its independent bottlers, whose plants and people sit on their own books; companies in which it holds sizeable stakes, including several large bottlers, had combined revenue of about $102.8 billion in 2025. Coca-Cola also owns some bottling, and PepsiCo also sells concentrate to franchise bottlers. Neither model is simply better; each pays for a different kind of control.
